Analysis of variance

Because each subject performed several movements in every condition, the raw rows are not independent observations. The data are therefore aggregated to one mean value per subject and condition, which yields r nrow(subj_means) subject-by-condition means before running the models.

#| label: aggregate-subjectssubj_means <- results_clean %>%  group_by(GROUP, SUBJ, ORI, DIR) %>%  summarise(    mean_mt  = mean(MovementTime),    mean_nvp = mean(NbVelPeaks),    .groups  = "drop"  )glimpse(subj_means)

A mixed ANOVA is fitted for movement time, with GROUP as between-subject factor and ORI and DIR as within-subject factors:

#| label: anova-mtmt_aov <- aov(mean_mt ~ GROUP * ORI * DIR + Error(SUBJ / (ORI * DIR)), data = subj_means)summary(mt_aov)

The same model is fitted for the number of velocity peaks:

#| label: anova-nvpnvp_aov <- aov(mean_nvp ~ GROUP * ORI * DIR + Error(SUBJ / (ORI * DIR)), data = subj_means)summary(nvp_aov)

Each Error: block of the output corresponds to one stratum of the design. The GROUP effect is tested in the Error: SUBJ block; ORI and its interaction with GROUP are tested in the Error: SUBJ:ORI block; DIR and its interaction with GROUP are tested in the Error: SUBJ:DIR block; and the remaining interactions are tested in the Error: SUBJ:ORI:DIR block. An effect is considered statistically significant when its p value, listed under Pr(>F), is below .05.

Results

Movement time. The ANOVA revealed a highly significant main effect of GROUP, F(2, 48) = 53.79, p < .001: the pp group was much slower (M = 4.38 s) than the ap group (M = 1.51 s) and the cp group (M = 1.08 s). Movement direction also had a significant main effect, F(1, 48) = 11.55, p = .001, with outward movements (M = 2.60 s) taking longer than inward movements (M = 2.23 s). This direction effect interacted with GROUP, F(2, 48) = 4.09, p = .023: the outward-minus-inward difference was much larger in the pp group (+0.77 s) than in the ap group (+0.17 s) and the cp group (+0.10 s). Target orientation did not significantly affect movement time overall, F(4, 192) = 1.64, p = .166, but interacted with GROUP, F(8, 192) = 1.99, p = .049, and entered a significant three-way GROUP × ORI × DIR interaction, F(8, 192) = 2.22, p = .027, indicating that the joint pattern of orientation and direction effects was not the same in all three groups.

Number of velocity peaks. The same model applied to the number of velocity peaks showed a highly significant GROUP effect, F(2, 48) = 35.31, p < .001: movements of the pp group contained far more velocity peaks (M = 12.90) than those of the ap group (M = 3.96) and the cp group (M = 3.19), reflecting much less smooth movements in the pp group. Target orientation had a significant main effect, F(4, 192) = 12.13, p < .001, with the highest number of peaks for the N orientation (M = 8.22) and the lowest for NW (M = 6.12), and this orientation effect interacted with GROUP, F(8, 192) = 3.25, p = .002. Movement direction had a smaller but significant effect, F(1, 48) = 4.45, p = .040, with more peaks for outward movements (M = 7.50) than inward movements (M = 6.51); the DIR × GROUP interaction was not significant, F(2, 48) = 1.84, p = .169, nor was the ORI × DIR interaction, F(4, 192) = 2.17, p = .075. The three-way GROUP × ORI × DIR interaction was significant, F(8, 192) = 2.37, p = .019.

Taken together, the pp group stands out on both dependent variables: slower, direction-sensitive movements and much less smooth trajectories, whereas the ap and cp groups behave similarly to each other. Orientation effects were absent for movement time but clearly present for the number of velocity peaks, suggesting that movement smoothness, more than movement duration, depends on target direction.
